feed.description: Software engineering conversations: reliability, architecture, delivery, and the tradeoffs nobody puts in the blog post.
feed.title: Practical Systems

bullets: A good on-call rotation is designed so that waking up is rare — the goal is minimizing unnecessary disruptions by aligning alerting with actionable outcomes.
Alerting should be action-oriented rather than reactive, ensuring that every notification demands a specific, meaningful response.
Error budgets work when they change behavior — their effectiveness lies in driving operational decisions, not just tracking failures.
The framing of incident response determines the trade-offs teams make, and a clear mental model is essential for consistent decision-making.
PagerDuty’s incident response model assumes someone owns the page, but this ownership structure often overlooks the second-order effect of overburdening individuals.
Systems thinking reveals that on-call design is not just about tools but about the underlying assumptions about responsibility and response patterns.
Sentry-class tooling helps expose failure modes that are otherwise invisible — ignoring them leads to rebuilding systems from scratch later.
Adopting tools like Linear or Datadog in incident workflows makes trade-offs visible, and failing to internalize them results in repeated, avoidable work.
